docs.title: Open Data Stack (odctl)
docs.text: odctl is a command-line tool that runs an open data stack on your machine with Docker Compose. You name the profiles you want, such as kafka-lite or airflow, and odctl starts them together with the services they depend on.

docs.title: Why not plain Docker Compose?
docs.text:
odctl is Docker Compose: it runs Compose files and selects services with Compose profiles. For one small project with two or three services, a Compose file of your own is enough. odctl helps when there are more.

  • One set of files for every project. Projects need different tools. One uses MLflow, Feast and Airflow, and another does not need Airflow. Copied compose files drift apart, for example when an image is upgraded in one copy only. odctl keeps the files in one place. Each release fixes the image versions and runs an end-to-end test for every profile, so a project pins an odctl version instead of keeping its own files.
  • The services are already connected. PostgreSQL creates the databases for MLflow, Feast and the others when it first starts. MLflow keeps its artifacts in S3 storage. Feast's config points to its registry in PostgreSQL, to Iceberg for offline features and to Valkey for online features. The Airflow image has the MLflow and Feast clients installed. Kafka Connect, Flink and Spark take connector jars with matching versions from one shared image.
  • Commands show what is running. odctl explain shows a profile's services, ports and dependencies. odctl up --dry-run shows what would start, in order. odctl ps lists the running containers with their health and ports. The CLI reference lists every command.

docs.title: What it runs
docs.text:
Area Technologies Messaging Kafka (KRaft), Karapace schema registry, Kafka Connect, Kafka UI (kafbat) Stream and batch processing Apache Flink, Apache Spark Analytics ClickHouse, Trino, Metabase Orchestration Apache Airflow, Temporal MLOps MLflow, Feast, Evidently Metadata and lineage OpenMetadata, Marquez Observability grafana/otel-lgtm (OpenTelemetry Collector, Prometheus, Tempo, Loki, Grafana) Storage and catalog PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector, pg_textsearch and PostGIS, SeaweedFS (S3), Iceberg REST catalog, Valkey Bundle, Apache Fluss

Kafka Connect comes with a set of connectors, such as the Iceberg sink and the Debezium PostgreSQL source. Kafka Connect lists them all.

docs.title: odctl up
docs.text:
Usage: odctl up [OPTIONS] {profiles}...

 Launch Open Data profiles.

 Resolves dependencies for the requested profiles and brings up the required
 Docker Compose stacks in the correct topological order.

 Refuses to start if the images for the resolved TAG are not published,
 naming the tag rather than leaving Docker to report a missing manifest.
 Warns about any service whose declared profile belongs to another compose
 file, since the planner will never start it.

│ *    profiles      <str>  One or more profiles to launch (e.g., 'ch-lite',   │
│                           'kafka-lite').                                     │
│                           [required]                                         │

│ --dry-run          Preview the execution plan without actually starting      │
│                    anything.                                                 │
│ --pull             Force pull the latest images from the registry before     │
│                    starting.                                                 │
│ --help             Show this message and exit.                               │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

   # Launch Clickhouse, Flink, and their dependencies

   $ odctl up ch-lite flink-lite


   # Preview what would be launched for Airflow

   $ odctl up airflow --dry-run


   # Force pull latest images before launching

   $ odctl up kafka-lite --pull

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: The recording shows the steps on this page: install odctl, preview a profile, start it, list the containers and stop them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Docker Engine or Docker Desktop, running. Give Docker 8 to 16 GB of memory.
  • Python 3.10 or later.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
odctl is a command-line tool, so install it into its own environment with uv or pipx.

uv tool install odctl
# or
pipx install odctl

pip install odctl also works.

docs.title: Create a workspace
docs.text:
odctl init

This copies the compose files and their settings into .odctl in the current directory, and writes .odctl/.env with TAG set to the CLI version. odctl reads from .odctl whenever it exists, so you can edit any file there. Workspace explains what changes with and without it, and how to customise it.

docs.title: Start a profile
docs.text:
List the profiles, then see what one of them starts:

odctl list
odctl up kafka-lite --dry-run

The dry run prints which compose files and profiles it would start:

Start it:

odctl up kafka-lite

odctl starts the profiles kafka-lite depends on first, then Kafka. It waits until the services are running, and healthy where they define a health check. odctl explain kafka-lite prints its addresses, and the Messaging page lists the same.

Check what is running, and stop everything when you are done:

odctl ps --all
odctl down --all

odctl down removes the containers, and the data inside them goes with them. See How it works.

docs.title: Use it with an AI assistant
docs.text: The docs site publishes llms.txt, an index of these pages for AI assistants, and llms-full.txt with every page in one file. The repository also has an odctl skill in skills/odctl/SKILL.md, generated from the profiles, which tells an assistant which profile to start and how to reach each service. For Claude Code, copy the skills/odctl folder into ~/.claude/skills/.

docs.title: What odctl up does
docs.text:
Take odctl up flink-lite as an example. Flink keeps its tables in Iceberg, so it needs the Iceberg REST catalog. The catalog keeps its metadata in PostgreSQL and its files in SeaweedFS. All of them need the shared jars in deps.

odctl reads these links from registry.yml and starts the profiles from left to right:

  1. deps copies connectors and jars into a shared Docker volume, creates the odctl network, and exits.
  2. postgres and storage start, and odctl waits until they are healthy.
  3. catalog starts once both are healthy.
  4. flink-lite starts last.

odctl up flink-lite --dry-run prints this plan without starting anything. Each profile page lists what its profile also starts.

docs.title: Dependencies and the start order
docs.text:
Each profile lists the profiles it needs under depends_on in registry.yml. odctl follows those lists from the profiles you name, one level at a time, until no new profile appears. It then sorts the result: deps first, postgres and storage next, catalog after them, and every other profile last, in alphabetical order.

The profiles are then grouped by compose file, in that order, and each file is started with one docker compose up --wait. That call returns once every service it started is running, and healthy where it has a health check, so a file starts only after the files before it are ready. deps is the exception: it starts attached, because its init container copies the jars and exits, and --wait treats an exiting container as a failure.

docs.title: Before anything starts
docs.text:
odctl up checks four things before it starts a container:

  1. Docker is reachable. If not, it stops.
  2. Every profile you name is in registry.yml. An unknown name stops it, with the name in the error.
  3. Every service can be started. A service that declares a profile owned by another compose file would never start, so odctl warns about it and carries on.
  4. odctl's own images exist for the tag. It resolves TAG as compose does and asks the registry for each odctl image that is not already on your machine. If the registry says one is missing, odctl stops and names the tag, rather than leaving Docker to fail on one service. If the registry cannot be reached, it starts anyway, so a machine with no network can run images it pulled before.

docs.title: Which containers a command touches
docs.text:
down, ps, logs, restart and recreate act only on the profiles you name, not on their dependencies. odctl down flink-lite stops Flink and leaves PostgreSQL, SeaweedFS and the catalog running for other profiles. odctl finds the containers by their compose labels: the project name starts with odctl-, and the service belongs to one of the named profiles.

There is one exception. When a profile depends on another profile in the same compose file, both are included, because compose refuses a command on a service whose dependency is left out. odctl down --volumes removes the shared deps volume and the odctl network only when no other profile has a container left.

docs.title: How you reach a service
docs.text:
Every service publishes its ports on the host at 127.0.0.1 only, so a browser or client on your machine uses http://127.0.0.1:<port>, and other machines on your network cannot reach them. This works the same on macOS, Linux and WSL2: Docker Desktop forwards the port to the host's 127.0.0.1, and WSL2 forwards it to Windows' localhost. To open a port to your network, remove 127.0.0.1: from its line in .odctl/compose-*.yml and run odctl recreate <profile>. Each profile page lists the ports.

Inside Docker, services reach each other by name on the odctl network, for example http://catalog:8181 or broker-1:19092 for Kafka. A container of your own reaches them the same way when it joins that network:

docker run --rm --network odctl curlimages/curl http://catalog:8181/v1/config

docs.title: Where data lives
docs.text:
Services keep their data inside their containers.

Command Containers Your data odctl restart kept kept odctl recreate replaced lost odctl down removed lost odctl down --volumes removed, with the odctl-shared-deps volume lost

So a database, a bucket, a topic or an Iceberg table lasts until the profile is stopped. This keeps every odctl up a clean start. The odctl-shared-deps volume holds only jars, so keeping it makes the next start faster.

docs.title: Which images run
docs.text:
Most services run their project's official image, pinned to an exact version. odctl builds five images of its own and publishes them to ghcr.io/jaehyeon-kim/odctl/:

Image Contents deps Connectors, jars and the Prometheus JMX agent, including the Iceberg REST catalog and the Kafka Connect Iceberg sink postgres PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector, pg_textsearch and PostGIS airflow Airflow with the MLflow and Feast clients and the model runtimes mlflow The MLflow server and model server with the model runtimes spark Spark with the Python clients jobs use

These five are tagged with the CLI version through TAG. Workspace explains how TAG is set with and without odctl init.

docs.title: Workspace
docs.text: odctl runs from one of two places: the files bundled with the CLI, or a workspace that odctl init copies them into.

docs.title: With and without odctl init
docs.text:
Without a workspace With a workspace Files odctl reads the compose files and registry.yml inside the installed package the copies in .odctl in the current directory Image tag of odctl's own images the CLI version the CLI version, written to .odctl/.env as TAG Your changes none; the package is replaced on every upgrade any file in .odctl After a CLI upgrade new files and images at once the old files and images, with a warning on every command until odctl init --force

A TAG set in the shell overrides both.

odctl looks for .odctl in the current directory. --workspace PATH points it at another directory, so one workspace can serve several projects.

docs.title: Customise it
docs.text:
odctl init copies everything odctl runs into .odctl. It copies only files that are missing, so running it again keeps your edits.

File What to change compose-*.yml Host ports, memory limits and environment variables of each service registry.yml The profiles, their compose files and their dependencies .env TAG, extra Python packages for Airflow (_AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS) and the MLflow services (_MLOPS_PIP_DEPS), and the model the MLflow model server serves (MODEL_URI) grafana/dashboards/ The Grafana dashboard for each service trino/rules.json Trino's file-based access control evidently/config.yaml The Evidently server's settings

docs.title: Apply a change
docs.text: A restart keeps the container, so it does not apply an edited compose file or .env. Run odctl recreate <profile> to replace the profile's containers from their current definition, and add --pull to fetch images again. Recreating discards the data in those containers. odctl restart <profile> is enough for files a service reads when it starts, such as trino/rules.json and the Grafana dashboards.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Each example edits the workspace, then applies the change. sed -i.bak works with both GNU and macOS sed, and keeps the original as a .bak file.

Give SeaweedFS 2 GB instead of 512 MB, for example when several projects share it. SeaweedFS is a Go program, and GOMEMLIMIT is a soft memory limit: as the memory the Go runtime manages nears it, the garbage collector runs more often and returns memory to the system sooner. It is three quarters of mem_limit, so change both:

sed -i.bak -e '/^  seaweed:/,/^  [a-z]/ s/mem_limit: 512m/mem_limit: 2g/' \
  -e '/^  seaweed:/,/^  [a-z]/ s/GOMEMLIMIT: 384MiB/GOMEMLIMIT: 1536MiB/' .odctl/compose-infra.yml
odctl recreate storage
docker inspect seaweed --format '{{.HostConfig.Memory}}'   # 2147483648

Publish Trino on port 8180 instead of 8080, when another program already uses 8080:

sed -i.bak 's/"127.0.0.1:8080:8080" # Trino/"127.0.0.1:8180:8080" # Trino/' .odctl/compose-analytics.yml
odctl up trino
docker port trino   # 8080/tcp -> 127.0.0.1:8180

Install extra Python packages in the Airflow container, for DAGs that import them:

sed -i.bak 's/^_AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS=.*/_AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS="dateparser==1.4.3"/' .odctl/.env
odctl up airflow
docker exec airflow python -c "import dateparser"

_AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS and _MLOPS_PIP_DEPS both install their packages from PyPI again in every new container: at the first odctl up, after odctl recreate, and after odctl down and odctl up. _AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS is for the Airflow containers. _MLOPS_PIP_DEPS is for the mlflow and mlflow-serve containers, for example a library a served model needs to load. odctl restart keeps the container, so the packages stay. Each new container needs PyPI, and pinned versions (transformers==5.20.2) keep the installed packages the same. MODEL_URI in the same file sets the model mlflow-serve serves, as MLflow tracking and model serving shows.

Create a bucket before its profile exists, for example for a project that has no profile. seaweed-init creates a fixed list of buckets, and .odctl/seaweed/s3.json gives the login user the Admin action, which creating a bucket needs. This runs boto3 in a container on the odctl network, where seaweed:8333 resolves, and prints the buckets, which now include desflow:

docs/snippets/storage/commands.sh:create-bucket
docker run --rm -i --network odctl python:3.12-slim \
  sh -c 'pip install -q --root-user-action=ignore boto3==1.43.118 && python -' <<'PY'
import boto3
s3 = boto3.client("s3", endpoint_url="http://seaweed:8333", region_name="us-east-1",
                  aws_access_key_id="user", aws_secret_access_key="password")
s3.create_bucket(Bucket="desflow")
print(sorted(b["Name"] for b in s3.list_buckets()["Buckets"]))
PY

Two other ways exist. weed shell inside the seaweed container runs s3.bucket.create -name desflow, the command seaweed-init runs. Adding the name to BUCKETS in .odctl/compose-infra.yml creates it at every start of the storage profile, but odctl init --force, which an upgrade needs, removes the edit.

docs.title: Trino access rules
docs.text: The shipped trino/rules.json grants every identity full table privileges and denies analyst schema ownership. Add your own table rules there for row filtering and column masking, then restart Trino.

docs.title: Start again
docs.text: odctl init --force deletes .odctl and copies the bundled files again, with TAG set to the current CLI version. Your edits are lost, so it asks for confirmation first.

docs.title: Labs
docs.text:
Work in progress. A series of labs takes one generated dataset of web events and logs for five tenants through Kafka, Flink, ClickHouse, Spark, Trino and the MLOps tools, each lab building on the one before. The code will be in benchtop, and each lab will be listed here as it is published.

Until then, the guides show each technology on its own.

docs.title: Containers exit or Docker runs out of memory
docs.text: Each service has a memory limit, listed on its profile page. The limits of everything you start add up, and Docker needs that much memory available. Give Docker 8 to 16 GB, start fewer profiles at once, or choose a lite profile over a full one. To lower a limit, edit mem_limit in the compose file in .odctl and run odctl recreate <profile>.

docs.title: Uploads fail with HTTP 500 and seaweed exited with code 137
docs.text: seaweed reached its memory limit while it buffered a large upload, and the kernel killed it. The client sees HTTP 500 and every profile that uses S3 loses its storage until the container starts again. docker inspect seaweed --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' prints true after such a kill. odctl sets GOMEMLIMIT in compose-infra.yml to three quarters of mem_limit, so SeaweedFS collects garbage more often as it nears the limit; a workspace made by an earlier release lacks it until odctl init --force. A model or file of several hundred MB can still reach the limit. Raise mem_limit and GOMEMLIMIT together, as How it works shows for 2 GB, and run odctl recreate storage.

docs.title: A port is already in use
docs.text: Every service publishes fixed host ports, listed on its profile page. If another program holds one, odctl up fails to start that service. Stop the other program, or change the host side of the port mapping in .odctl/compose-*.yml and run odctl recreate <profile>. Containers still reach each other on their internal ports, so only clients on your host need the new port.

docs.title: Use 127.0.0.1, not localhost
docs.text: Host addresses in odctl explain and on these pages use 127.0.0.1. With IPv6 enabled in Docker, localhost can resolve to a service's IPv6 address, and services that listen on IPv4 only reset the connection. localhost works when Docker's IPv6 is off.

docs.title: No published image for a TAG
docs.text:
odctl up checks the images odctl builds before it starts anything. If the registry says an image for the resolved TAG does not exist, it stops with No published image for TAG=... and lists the missing images. An image already on your machine passes without a registry call. If the registry cannot be reached, odctl starts anyway and Docker reports what it finds.

The usual causes are a CLI version whose images are not published yet, or a TAG in .odctl/.env that you changed by hand. Set TAG to a published version in .odctl/.env, or install a CLI version whose images exist.

docs.title: Workspace TAG differs from the CLI version
docs.text: After you upgrade the CLI, every command except odctl init warns that .odctl/.env sets an older TAG. The workspace keeps the old profiles, images and compose files until you run odctl init --force, which also resets your edits.

docs.title: A service is up but does not work
docs.text: odctl logs <profile> shows the logs of a profile's containers. Add -s <service> for one service, or -f to follow them. odctl ps --all shows every container odctl manages and its state.

docs.title: Older messages are missing
docs.text: The Kafka brokers delete messages after one day, or when a partition passes 500 MB. A consumer that starts from the beginning of a topic sees only what is left. Keep messages longer shows how to read these limits and how to set retention.ms and retention.bytes to -1 on a topic that must keep everything.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: Each release, newest first: what changed, then under Upgrading what to change in commands, workspaces or clients that use the previous release. Releases up to 1.0.2 are described on GitHub Releases.

docs.title: Version 1.2.0
docs.text:
Flink can send rows to an HTTP API, Spark reads Kafka with no extra options, SeaweedFS survives uploads of large models, and the guides cover cases that real projects met.

  • Flink's SQL client has the HTTP connector. Send rows to an HTTP API pushes a feature value to Feast.
  • Spark has the Kafka connector and the Avro module, so a job reads a topic, including Avro records written with the schema registry, with no --packages option. See Read a Kafka topic and Read Avro records written with the schema registry.
  • Keep messages longer shows the broker's one-day and 500 MB retention and how to turn both off for a topic. Troubleshooting lists the symptom.
  • seaweed sets GOMEMLIMIT to three quarters of its memory limit, so uploads of a model of a few hundred MB no longer end with HTTP 500 and a killed container. Troubleshooting says what to do when the limit is still reached, and How it works changes both values together.
  • The MLflow guide has three new sections: Move the alias to a new version, which needs odctl restart mlflow, Load a model from your machine and Serve a model that reads online features.
  • The text on _MLOPS_PIP_DEPS now says that every new mlflow and mlflow-serve container installs the packages from PyPI again. How it works and the MLflow guide have the details.
  • How it works shows how to create a bucket before its profile exists.
  • Several rolling windows shows that Flink SQL refuses two different OVER windows in one streaming query, and the two ways around it.
  • The Evidently guide says what Evidently does not estimate and why NannyML needs Python 3.12.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: • A workspace made by odctl init with an earlier release keeps its old compose-infra.yml, which has no GOMEMLIMIT for seaweed. Run odctl init --force to copy the new files; it replaces your edits, so keep a copy of them. Then run odctl recreate storage.

docs.title: Version 1.1.0
docs.text:
Every service is now reachable from your machine only, and the docs have a Roadmap and a Changelog.

  • Every published port binds to 127.0.0.1, on macOS, Linux and WSL2, so other machines on your network cannot reach the services. How you reach a service says how to open a port when you need to.
  • Kafka no longer publishes ports 29092, 29093 and 29094, which were listeners for a minikube cluster.
  • An odctl skill and llms.txt help an AI assistant choose a profile and reach its services. See Use it with an AI assistant.
  • Eight guides show in a diagram how data moves between their services, and How it works shows what odctl up checks and the order it starts services in. The end-to-end tests run every command the guides show.
  • The tables of odctl ps and odctl explain draw straight right borders on rows with port mappings.
  • odctl down --help says what --volumes removes.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
• To reach a service from another machine, run odctl init, remove 127.0.0.1: from the service's port line in .odctl/compose-*.yml, and run odctl recreate <profile>.
  • A Kafka client in minikube cannot use host.minikube.internal:29092 any more. Add a listener for it to the Kafka service in .odctl/compose-kafka.yml.
  • A workspace made by odctl init with an earlier release keeps its old compose files, which publish on all interfaces and include port 29092. Run odctl init --force to copy the new files; it replaces your edits.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: The work comes in the order shown, without dates: a release ships when it is ready. Features come first, then the testing and setup work that adds no feature. Each planned item links to its GitHub issue where one exists.

Tools for AI agents that show the profiles and what is running, with up and down behind a setting. #141

docs.title: Released
docs.text:
Newest first.

1.2.0: Streaming

Flink writes to HTTP APIs such as Feast's push endpoint, Spark reads Kafka without downloading packages, and guides to Kafka retention and to several rolling windows in Flink SQL. The release also fixes the MLflow and storage guides and sets GOMEMLIMIT, a soft limit for the Go runtime, on seaweed, so large model uploads do not hit its container memory limit.

odctl is tested on Python 3.15, ZooKeeper and Metabase are updated, and Renovate groups image updates by compose file.

What each release changed is in the Changelog and on GitHub Releases.

docs.title: Airflow DAGs from S3
docs.text:
The airflow profile runs airflow standalone in one container against odctl's PostgreSQL. It reads DAG files from s3://airflow/dags on SeaweedFS, so you deploy a DAG by uploading it. No volume or sync container is involved. The end-to-end tests run the steps below on every release.

odctl up airflow

The web UI is at http://127.0.0.1:8085, with user user and password password.

docs.title: Upload a DAG
docs.text:
Any S3 client pointed at http://127.0.0.1:8333 with key user and secret password can upload. This uses boto3 inside the Airflow container:

docs/snippets/airflow-dags/commands.sh:upload
docker exec -i airflow python - <<'PY'
import boto3
body = '''
from airflow.sdk import DAG
from airflow.providers.standard.operators.bash import BashOperator
import pendulum

with DAG(
    dag_id="hello",
    start_date=pendulum.datetime(2026, 1, 1, tz="UTC"),
    schedule=None,
    catchup=False,
):
    BashOperator(task_id="say_hello", bash_command="echo hello")
'''
boto3.client("s3", endpoint_url="http://seaweed:8333").put_object(
    Bucket="airflow", Key="dags/hello.py", Body=body.encode())
PY

Airflow checks the bucket every 15 seconds and then parses the new file.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
New DAGs start paused. Wait until the DAG is listed, then unpause and trigger it:

docs/snippets/airflow-dags/commands.sh:run
docker exec airflow airflow dags list | grep hello
docker exec airflow airflow dags unpause hello
docker exec airflow airflow dags trigger hello
docker exec airflow airflow dags list-runs hello

The DAG page shows the run and the say_hello task.

docs.title: Plugins and packages
docs.text:
Plugins are copied from s3://airflow/plugins when the container starts, because Airflow loads plugins only once. Run odctl restart airflow after changing one.

To install extra Python packages, set _AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS in .odctl/.env, for example _AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS="scikit-learn", and run odctl recreate airflow. Tasks already have the MLflow and Feast clients, and MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI points at the mlflow profile.

docs.title: ClickHouse
docs.text:
The ch-lite profile runs one shard with two replicas, ch-11 and ch-12, coordinated by ClickHouse Keeper in ch-keeper. ch-full adds a second shard, ch-21 and ch-22. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

odctl up ch-lite
Endpoint Address HTTP from the host http://127.0.0.1:8123 (ch-11) and http://127.0.0.1:8124 (ch-12); ch-full adds 8125 (ch-21) and 8126 (ch-22) Native protocol from the host 127.0.0.1:9000 (ch-11) and 127.0.0.1:9001 (ch-12); ch-full adds 9002 (ch-21) and 9003 (ch-22) Users default and user, both with the password password

Every server creates the feature_store and odctl databases when it starts with no data.

docs.title: Create a table and query it
docs.text:
clickhouse-client is in each server container:

docs/snippets/clickhouse/commands.sh:merge-tree
docker exec ch-11 clickhouse-client --password password -q "SHOW DATABASES"

docker exec ch-11 clickhouse-client --password password -q \
  "CREATE TABLE default.demo (id UInt32) ENGINE=MergeTree ORDER BY id"
docker exec ch-11 clickhouse-client --password password -q \
  "INSERT INTO default.demo SELECT number FROM numbers(10)"
docker exec ch-11 clickhouse-client --password password -q \
  "SELECT count() FROM default.demo"

The last command prints 10.

ClickHouse also serves a query page at http://127.0.0.1:8123/play. Enter default and password in the top right, write a query and press Run.

docs.title: Replicate across the cluster
docs.text:
In ch-full, {cluster} names odctl_cluster, which has two shards of two replicas. A table created ON CLUSTER with ReplicatedMergeTree is created on all four servers, and Keeper keeps the two replicas of each shard in step:

docs/snippets/clickhouse/commands.sh:replicated
odctl up ch-full

docker exec ch-11 clickhouse-client --password password -q \
  "CREATE TABLE default.repl ON CLUSTER '{cluster}' (id UInt32) ENGINE=ReplicatedMergeTree ORDER BY id"
docker exec ch-11 clickhouse-client --password password -q \
  "INSERT INTO default.repl SELECT number FROM numbers(50)"

docker exec ch-12 clickhouse-client --password password -q "SELECT count() FROM default.repl"
docker exec ch-21 clickhouse-client --password password -q "SELECT count() FROM default.repl"

ch-12, the other replica of shard 1, returns 50 once replication has caught up. ch-21 returns 0, because shard 2 holds only the rows written to it.

In ch-lite, {cluster} names odctl_single_shard, which holds ch-11 and ch-12 only, so ON CLUSTER statements finish without waiting for the missing shard.

docs.title: From another container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, connect to ch-11:8123 over HTTP or ch-11:9000 with the native protocol, with the same users. Trino's clickhouse catalog reads the feature_store database on ch-11, as Trino and Metabase shows.

docs.title: Evidently reports
docs.text:
The evidently profile runs the Evidently UI and API. It keeps projects, reports, dashboards and datasets in the evidently database on PostgreSQL. The client computes each report and pushes the result. Evidently covers data drift and data quality. It gives no estimate of a model's performance while the outcomes are unknown. NannyML does, but version 0.13.1 supports Python 3.9 to 3.12 and the Airflow image runs Python 3.13, so run NannyML in a Python 3.12 process on your machine. The end-to-end tests run the code below on every release.

docs/snippets/evidently-reports/commands.sh:install
odctl up evidently
pip install evidently==0.7.23

The server runs Evidently 0.7.23, so install the same client version. The UI is at http://127.0.0.1:8089, with no login.

docs.title: Push a data drift report
docs.text:
docs/snippets/evidently-reports/steps.py:report
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from evidently import Report
from evidently.presets import DataDriftPreset
from evidently.ui.workspace import RemoteWorkspace

ws = RemoteWorkspace("http://127.0.0.1:8089")
project = ws.create_project("demo")

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
reference = pd.DataFrame({"x": rng.normal(0, 1, 500), "y": rng.normal(0, 1, 500)})
current = pd.DataFrame({"x": rng.normal(3, 1, 500), "y": rng.normal(0, 1, 500)})

snapshot = Report([DataDriftPreset()]).run(current_data=current, reference_data=reference)
ws.add_run(project.id, snapshot)

Column x moves by three standard deviations and y does not, so the report in the UI shows one drifted column.

Open the report under the project's Reports tab:

docs.title: Store a dataset
docs.text:
docs/snippets/evidently-reports/steps.py:dataset
from evidently import DataDefinition, Dataset

data = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "score": [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]})
dataset_id = ws.add_dataset(project.id, Dataset.from_pandas(data, data_definition=DataDefinition()), "demo")
ws.load_dataset(dataset_id).as_dataframe()

The dataset is stored in the evidently database, with the projects and reports.

docs.title: From Airflow or another container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, connect with RemoteWorkspace("http://evidently:8000"). For Airflow tasks, set _AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS="evidently==0.7.23" in .odctl/.env and run odctl recreate airflow. The server's settings are in evidently/config.yaml in the workspace.

docs.title: Feast with Iceberg
docs.text:
The feast profile runs the Feast UI and the online feature server. Feast stores no feature values of its own. Feature definitions live in a SQL registry in PostgreSQL, offline values come from Iceberg tables through the REST catalog, and online values are served from Valkey. You run feast apply and the other client commands from your own environment. The end-to-end tests run the steps below on every release.

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/commands.sh:install
odctl up feast
pip install "feast[duckdb,iceberg,redis,postgres]==0.66.0" pyarrow

docs.title: Point the clients at the stack
docs.text:
PyIceberg, which Feast uses to read Iceberg, takes its catalog settings from the environment:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/commands.sh:catalog-env
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__TYPE=rest
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__URI=http://127.0.0.1:8181
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__WAREHOUSE=s3://warehouse/
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__S3__ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:8333
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__S3__ACCESS_KEY_ID=user
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__S3__SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=password
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__S3__PATH_STYLE_ACCESS=true
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__S3__REGION=us-east-1

docs.title: Create an Iceberg table
docs.text:
docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/steps.py:create-table
import datetime, pyarrow as pa
from pyiceberg.catalog import load_catalog

cat = load_catalog("odctl")
cat.create_namespace_if_not_exists("demo")
schema = pa.schema([
    pa.field("driver_id", pa.int64(), nullable=False),
    pa.field("event_timestamp", pa.timestamp("us", tz="UTC"), nullable=False),
    pa.field("conv_rate", pa.float32(), nullable=False),
])
t = cat.create_table("demo.driver_stats", schema=schema)
now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).replace(microsecond=0)
t.append(pa.Table.from_pydict({
    "driver_id": [1001, 1002],
    "event_timestamp": [now - datetime.timedelta(hours=1)] * 2,
    "conv_rate": [0.5, 0.75],
}, schema=schema))

docs.title: Define the feature repository
docs.text:
feature_repo/feature_store.yaml:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/feature_repo/feature_store.yaml
project: demo
provider: local
registry:
  registry_type: sql
  path: postgresql+psycopg://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/feast
offline_store:
  type: duckdb
online_store:
  type: redis
  connection_string: "127.0.0.1:6379,username=user,password=password"
entity_key_serialization_version: 3

feature_repo/definitions.py:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/feature_repo/definitions.py
from datetime import timedelta
from feast import Entity, FeatureView, Field
from feast.types import Float32
from feast.infra.data_sources.contrib.iceberg_catalog.iceberg_source import IcebergSource

driver = Entity(name="driver", join_keys=["driver_id"])
src = IcebergSource(
    warehouse="", namespace="demo", table="driver_stats",
    catalog_type="rest", catalog_name="odctl",
    endpoint="http://127.0.0.1:8181",
    timestamp_field="event_timestamp",
)
fv = FeatureView(
    name="driver_stats", entities=[driver], ttl=timedelta(days=365),
    schema=[Field(name="conv_rate", dtype=Float32)], source=src, online=True,
)

Pass warehouse="" and catalog_name="odctl". Feast's REST client puts the warehouse into the URL path, and the catalog serves its API with no prefix, so a real warehouse value fails with HTTP 400.

docs.title: Register and materialise
docs.text:
docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/commands.sh:apply-materialize
feast -c feature_repo apply
feast -c feature_repo materialize-incremental "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S)"

FeatureStore(repo_path="feature_repo").get_historical_features(...) now takes a point-in-time join from Iceberg through DuckDB, and get_online_features(...) reads the materialised values from Valkey.

docs.title: Serve from the stack
docs.text:
The UI at http://127.0.0.1:8890 and the online feature server at http://127.0.0.1:6566 load their repository from s3://feast/repo. To serve your features, upload the repository there with container addresses in its feature_store.yaml: postgres:5432, valkey:6379 and http://catalog:8181. The services check that prefix every 15 seconds and restart Feast when it changes.

Once the repository is uploaded, the UI lists the project and its feature views:

docs.title: Flink SQL: Kafka to PostgreSQL
docs.text:
The flink-lite profile runs a Flink JobManager, one TaskManager and the SQL Gateway. flink-full runs three TaskManagers. Flink's connector jars for Kafka, Avro with the schema registry, JDBC, Iceberg and HTTP come from the shared volume that the deps profile fills. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide reads Avro records from Kafka through the Karapace schema registry and writes an aggregate to PostgreSQL over JDBC. Ingest into Iceberg shows Flink writing an Iceberg table.

odctl up flink-lite kafka-lite

flink-lite starts PostgreSQL itself, because it depends on the Iceberg catalog, which keeps its metadata there.

Endpoint Address Flink UI and REST API from the host http://127.0.0.1:8082 SQL Gateway REST API from the host http://127.0.0.1:8084 Flink REST API inside the odctl network http://jobmanager:8081 SQL Gateway inside the odctl network http://flink-sql-gateway:8083

docs.title: Create the topic and the target table
docs.text:
docs/snippets/flink-sql/commands.sh:create-topic-table
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --if-not-exists --topic orders --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1

docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  CREATE TABLE supplier_stats (supplier TEXT PRIMARY KEY, orders BIGINT, total DOUBLE PRECISION);"

docs.title: Run the SQL
docs.text:
Open the SQL client in the JobManager container:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/commands.sh:sql-client
docker exec -it flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh
docs/snippets/flink-sql/steps.sql:kafka-to-postgres
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
CREATE TABLE orders (supplier STRING, price DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='kafka','topic'='orders','properties.bootstrap.servers'='broker-1:19092','scan.startup.mode'='earliest-offset','scan.bounded.mode'='latest-offset','format'='avro-confluent','avro-confluent.url'='http://karapace:8081');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES ('a', 10.0), ('a', 5.0), ('b', 7.5);
CREATE TABLE stats (supplier STRING, orders BIGINT, total DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY (supplier) NOT ENFORCED) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='supplier_stats','username'='user','password'='password');
INSERT INTO stats SELECT supplier, COUNT(*), SUM(price) FROM orders GROUP BY supplier;

The first INSERT writes three Avro records to Kafka and registers their schema in Karapace. The second reads them back, groups them by supplier and writes the result to PostgreSQL. scan.bounded.mode set to latest-offset makes the Kafka source stop at the end of the topic, so the batch job finishes. Leave it out and set execution.runtime-mode to streaming for a job that keeps running.

Right after Kafka starts, Karapace can answer its health check and still time out on a schema write for a short while. If the first INSERT fails on the schema registry, run it again.

docs.title: Check the result
docs.text:
docs/snippets/flink-sql/commands.sh:check
docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "SELECT * FROM supplier_stats ORDER BY supplier"

Supplier a has 2 orders totalling 15, and supplier b has 1 order totalling 7.5. The Flink UI at http://127.0.0.1:8082 shows the jobs the SQL client submitted.

The two INSERT statements run as two batch jobs, listed under Completed Jobs.

docs.title: Send rows to an HTTP API
docs.text:
The HTTP connector sends rows to a URL. This section pushes a feature value to Feast, which takes it at /push and serves it from its online store.

odctl up feast

Feast needs a push source before it accepts a push. Save these definitions as definitions.py:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/definitions.py
from datetime import timedelta
from feast import Entity, FeatureView, Field, FileSource, PushSource
from feast.types import Float32, Int64
from feast.value_type import ValueType

driver = Entity(name="driver", join_keys=["driver_id"], value_type=ValueType.INT64)
# Nothing reads this file. A push source needs a batch source behind it.
batch = FileSource(path="/tmp/driver_stats.parquet", timestamp_field="event_timestamp")
push = PushSource(name="driver_stats_push", batch_source=batch)
driver_stats = FeatureView(
    name="driver_stats",
    entities=[driver],
    ttl=timedelta(days=1),
    schema=[Field(name="driver_id", dtype=Int64), Field(name="conv_rate", dtype=Float32)],
    source=push,
    online=True,
)

Copy the definitions into the Feast container and apply them. --skip-source-validation stops Feast from looking for the file behind the batch source:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/commands.sh:feast-apply
docker cp definitions.py feast-serve:/tmp/feature_repo/definitions.py
docker exec feast-serve feast -c /tmp/feature_repo apply --skip-source-validation

Open the SQL client as above and run these statements:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/steps.sql:feast-push
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
CREATE TABLE feast_push (
  push_source_name STRING,
  df ROW<driver_id ARRAY<BIGINT>, conv_rate ARRAY<DOUBLE>, event_timestamp ARRAY<TIMESTAMP_LTZ(3)>>,
  allow_registry_cache BOOLEAN
) WITH (
  'connector' = 'http-async-sink',
  'url' = 'http://feast-serve:6566/push',
  'format' = 'json',
  'http.sink.writer.request.mode' = 'single',
  'http.sink.header.Content-Type' = 'application/json'
);
INSERT INTO feast_push SELECT 'driver_stats_push', ROW(ARRAY[CAST(1001 AS BIGINT)], ARRAY[CAST(0.9 AS DOUBLE)], ARRAY[CURRENT_TIMESTAMP]), FALSE;

The connector is http-async-sink. Its default sends rows in batches as one JSON array. Feast's /push takes one JSON object, so http.sink.writer.request.mode is single, which sends one request for each row. The sink sends no Content-Type header, and Feast answers 422 without one, so http.sink.header.Content-Type sets it. The column names are the field names of the request body. Feast reads df as a table of columns, so each field holds an array.

Feast caches its registry for up to a minute after apply. allow_registry_cache set to FALSE makes the push read the registry again, so it works at once. The timestamp must be new: a push with the same event_timestamp as the stored value does not replace it, so the statement uses CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.

The Flink job finishes and prints Complete execution even when Feast rejects the request. The failure is only in the TaskManager log as Http Sink failed to write. Read the value back from Feast to check the push:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/commands.sh:feast-read
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6566/get-online-features \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"features": ["driver_stats:conv_rate"], "entities": {"driver_id": [1001]}}'

The answer holds 0.8999999761581421 for conv_rate, which is 0.9 as a 32-bit float. The read also uses the cached registry, so right after apply it can answer that the feature view does not exist. Run it again after a minute.

docs.title: Several rolling windows
docs.text:
A feature such as the sum of a card's payments over 10 minutes, 1 hour and 1 day needs one rolling window for each size. A streaming query cannot hold two different OVER windows. Flink's documentation says that for streaming queries the OVER windows of all aggregates in one SELECT must be identical (Over aggregation, Flink 2.2). Run this in the SQL client to see Flink refuse a query with a 10 minute and a 1 hour window:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/steps.sql:windows-refused
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'streaming';
CREATE TABLE payments (card BIGINT, amount DOUBLE, seq BIGINT, ts AS TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(seq * 60000, 3), WATERMARK FOR ts AS ts) WITH ('connector'='datagen','fields.seq.kind'='sequence','fields.seq.start'='1','fields.seq.end'='20','fields.card.min'='1','fields.card.max'='2','fields.amount.min'='1','fields.amount.max'='10');
SELECT card,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '10' MINUTE PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS sum_10m,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1' HOUR PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS sum_1h
FROM payments;

The client prints [ERROR] Could not execute SQL statement. with this reason:

org.apache.flink.table.api.TableException: Over Agg: Unsupported use of OVER windows. All aggregates must be computed on the same window. please re-check the over window statement.

The first route is one statement for each window size, each writing its own table. Create the two PostgreSQL tables:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/commands.sh:create-window-tables
docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  CREATE TABLE card_sum_10m (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE PRECISION);
  CREATE TABLE card_sum_1h (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE PRECISION);"

Then run the two statements in a new SQL client session. The sequence field makes the source stop after 20 rows, and the event time ts makes each job write every row before it finishes. An OVER window on PROCTIME() would lose the rows still waiting for their timer when a bounded source ends:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/steps.sql:windows-one-per-size
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'streaming';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
CREATE TABLE payments (card BIGINT, amount DOUBLE, seq BIGINT, ts AS TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(seq * 60000, 3), WATERMARK FOR ts AS ts) WITH ('connector'='datagen','fields.seq.kind'='sequence','fields.seq.start'='1','fields.seq.end'='20','fields.card.min'='1','fields.card.max'='2','fields.amount.min'='1','fields.amount.max'='10');
CREATE TABLE sum_10m (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='card_sum_10m','username'='user','password'='password');
CREATE TABLE sum_1h (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='card_sum_1h','username'='user','password'='password');
INSERT INTO sum_10m SELECT card, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '10' MINUTE PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) FROM payments;
INSERT INTO sum_1h SELECT card, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1' HOUR PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) FROM payments;

Each table holds 20 rows:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/commands.sh:check-windows
docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM card_sum_10m) AS rows_10m, (SELECT count(*) FROM card_sum_1h) AS rows_1h"

The cost is one job for each window size, each reading the source again, and one table for each size that a reader has to join on the key. With four sizes that is four jobs.

The second route is one KeyedProcessFunction in the DataStream API, which keeps the events of the longest window in Flink state and computes every size from them. This sketch is not run by the end-to-end tests:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/keyed_sketch.py:keyed-sketch
from pyflink.common import Types
from pyflink.datastream.functions import KeyedProcessFunction, RuntimeContext
from pyflink.datastream.state import ListStateDescriptor

WINDOWS_MS = {"10m": 600_000, "1h": 3_600_000, "1d": 86_400_000, "7d": 604_800_000}


class RollingSums(KeyedProcessFunction):
    def open(self, runtime_context: RuntimeContext):
        # Every event of the longest window, for each key, kept in Flink state.
        self.events = runtime_context.get_list_state(
            ListStateDescriptor("events", Types.TUPLE([Types.LONG(), Types.DOUBLE()]))
        )

    def process_element(self, value, ctx):
        now = ctx.timestamp()
        kept = [(t, a) for t, a in self.events.get() if now - t <= WINDOWS_MS["7d"]]
        kept.append((now, value[1]))
        self.events.update(kept)
        yield value[0], {n: sum(a for t, a in kept if now - t <= ms) for n, ms in WINDOWS_MS.items()}

One job computes all sizes, but you write and test the code in Python or Java instead of SQL, and you manage the state, which grows with the events of the longest window for each key.

docs.text: Kafka Connect, Flink and Spark all write Iceberg tables through the same REST catalog, http://catalog:8181, with the files on SeaweedFS under s3://warehouse. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

docs.title: Kafka Connect sink
docs.text:
kafka-lite does not start the catalog, so start both:

odctl up kafka-lite catalog

Create a namespace and a table through the catalog's REST API:

docs/snippets/iceberg-ingestion/commands.sh:create-table
api=http://127.0.0.1:8181/v1/namespaces
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"namespace":["demo"]}' "$api"
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"kc","schema":{"type":"struct","schema-id":0,"fields":[{"id":1,"name":"id","required":false,"type":"long"},{"id":2,"name":"name","required":false,"type":"string"}]}}' \
  "$api/demo/tables"

Create the topic and the sink's control topic, then write some JSON records:

docs/snippets/iceberg-ingestion/commands.sh:topics-produce
for topic in demo-iceberg control-iceberg; do
  docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
    --create --if-not-exists --topic "$topic" --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
done
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do echo "{\"id\":$i,\"name\":\"n$i\"}"; done | docker exec -i kafka \
  /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 --topic demo-iceberg

Save the sink's configuration as demo-iceberg.json:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/demo-iceberg.json
{
  "name": "demo-iceberg",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "org.apache.iceberg.connect.IcebergSinkConnector",
    "tasks.max": "1",
    "topics": "demo-iceberg",
    "value.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.json.JsonConverter",
    "value.converter.schemas.enable": "false",
    "key.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.StringConverter",
    "iceberg.tables": "demo.kc",
    "iceberg.control.commit.interval-ms": "10000",
    "iceberg.kafka.session.timeout.ms": "300000",
    "iceberg.kafka.heartbeat.interval.ms": "3000",
    "iceberg.kafka.auto.offset.reset": "earliest",
    "consumer.override.auto.offset.reset": "earliest",
    "iceberg.catalog.type": "rest",
    "iceberg.catalog.uri": "http://catalog:8181",
    "iceberg.catalog.io-impl": "org.apache.iceberg.aws.s3.S3FileIO",
    "iceberg.catalog.client.region": "us-east-1",
    "iceberg.catalog.s3.endpoint": "http://seaweed:8333",
    "iceberg.catalog.s3.path-style-access": "true",
    "iceberg.catalog.s3.access-key-id": "user",
    "iceberg.catalog.s3.secret-access-key": "password"
  }
}

Register it with Kafka Connect:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/commands.sh:register
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors -d @demo-iceberg.json

The first commit can take a minute or more, because the sink waits for its control consumer to join a group. After that, curl $api/demo/tables/kc shows a snapshot whose summary has "total-records": "5".

The table's data and metadata files are in SeaweedFS, whose browser at http://127.0.0.1:8889 lists the buckets, including warehouse.

docs.title: Kafka Connect
docs.text:
Both Kafka profiles run one Kafka Connect worker, connect, beside the brokers. It loads its plugins from the shared volume that the deps profile fills, and you manage connectors through its REST API. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

odctl up kafka-lite
Setting Value REST API from the host http://127.0.0.1:8083 REST API inside the odctl network http://connect:8083 Plugin folder /mnt/shared-deps/connect Default converters JSON with schemas, for keys and values Offset flush interval 10 seconds

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
The deps image puts these connectors in the plugin folder: the Apache Iceberg sink, the Debezium PostgreSQL source, the ClickHouse sink, the Aiven JDBC connector, the Aiven S3 sink, the Redis connector and the MSK data generator. List the classes Connect has loaded:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/commands.sh:plugins
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/connector-plugins

The tests check that the list includes org.apache.iceberg.connect.IcebergSinkConnector, io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector and com.clickhouse.kafka.connect.ClickHouseSinkConnector. A plugin missing from the volume does not stop Connect from starting. It only leaves the class out of this list.

docs.title: Register a connector
docs.text:
A connector is a name and a config object, posted to /connectors. Ingest into Iceberg has a complete Iceberg sink configuration. Save it as demo-iceberg.json and post it:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/commands.sh:register
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors -d @demo-iceberg.json

The worker's default converters expect JSON with a schema envelope. A connector that reads plain JSON sets "value.converter.schemas.enable": "false" in its own config, as the Iceberg example does.

docs.title: Check and remove it
docs.text:
docs/snippets/kafka-connect/commands.sh:status-remove
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors/demo-iceberg/status
curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors/demo-iceberg

The status shows the connector and each task as RUNNING or FAILED, with the error for a failed task. The worker's log has the rest:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/commands.sh:logs
docker logs --tail 40 connect

Kafka UI lists the connector under Kafka Connect, Connectors:

odctl up postgres kafka-lite

docs.title: Produce and consume with Kafka
docs.text:
The kafka-lite profile runs one Kafka broker in KRaft mode, the Karapace schema registry, Kafka Connect and Kafka UI. kafka-full runs three brokers with the same services beside them. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

odctl up kafka-lite
Endpoint Address Bootstrap servers from the host 127.0.0.1:9092 (kafka-full adds 127.0.0.1:9093 and 127.0.0.1:9094) Bootstrap servers inside the odctl network broker-1:19092 Kafka UI http://127.0.0.1:8086 Schema registry (Karapace) http://127.0.0.1:8081 Kafka Connect REST API http://127.0.0.1:8083

docs.title: Create a topic
docs.text:
The Kafka command-line tools are in the broker container, which is kafka in kafka-lite and kafka-1 in kafka-full:

docs/snippets/kafka/commands.sh:create-topic
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --topic demo --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1

docs.title: Produce and consume
docs.text:
docs/snippets/kafka/commands.sh:produce-consume
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do echo "{\"n\":$i}"; done | docker exec -i kafka \
  /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 --topic demo

docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --topic demo --from-beginning --max-messages 5 --timeout-ms 60000

The consumer reads through a consumer group, so its offsets are stored in the broker's __consumer_offsets topic.

Kafka UI at http://127.0.0.1:8086 shows the topics, their messages, the consumer groups and the schemas in Karapace.

docs.title: Keep messages longer
docs.text:
The brokers delete old messages. A partition keeps data for one day or up to 500 MB, and a segment is deleted once either limit is passed. The compose file sets both: KAFKA_LOG_RETENTION_MS is 86400000 and KAFKA_LOG_RETENTION_BYTES is 524288000. A topic created without settings takes these values:

docs/snippets/kafka/commands.sh:retention-default
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --describe --all --entity-type topics --entity-name demo | grep -E '^ *retention\.(ms|bytes)='

The output shows retention.ms=86400000 and retention.bytes=524288000. To keep everything in one topic, set retention.ms and retention.bytes to -1 when you create it. -1 means no limit. Other topics keep the broker defaults.

docs/snippets/kafka/commands.sh:retention-unlimited
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --topic history --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1 \
  --config retention.ms=-1 --config retention.bytes=-1

docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --describe --entity-type topics --entity-name history

The describe command lists the settings of that topic: retention.ms=-1 and retention.bytes=-1. retention.bytes applies to each partition, so a topic with three partitions at 500 MB can hold 1.5 GB. To change an existing topic, use kafka-configs.sh --alter --add-config with the same two settings. If older messages are missing, see Troubleshooting.
