docs.title: OpenLineage and Marquez
docs.text:
The lineage profile runs Marquez: an API that receives OpenLineage events and keeps jobs, runs and datasets on PostgreSQL, and a web UI that draws the lineage graph. Anything that sends OpenLineage events over HTTP can report to it. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

odctl up lineage
Endpoint Address Marquez API from the host http://127.0.0.1:5002 Marquez API inside the odctl network http://marquez-api:5000 Lineage graph UI http://127.0.0.1:3003

docs.title: Send OpenLineage events
docs.text:
A run is reported as a START event and a COMPLETE event with the same run id. The job reads one dataset and writes another:

docs/snippets/lineage/commands.sh:send
RUN_ID=a1b2c3d4-0000-4000-8000-000000000001
NOW=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.000Z)

for event in START COMPLETE; do
  curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5002/api/v1/lineage \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "{\"eventType\":\"$event\",\"eventTime\":\"$NOW\",
         \"producer\":\"demo\",
         \"run\":{\"runId\":\"$RUN_ID\"},
         \"job\":{\"namespace\":\"demo\",\"name\":\"demo-job\"},
         \"inputs\":[{\"namespace\":\"demo\",\"name\":\"raw-orders\"}],
         \"outputs\":[{\"namespace\":\"demo\",\"name\":\"demo-dataset\"}]}"
done

The run id is a UUID, as OpenLineage requires.

docs.title: Read the lineage back
docs.text:
docs/snippets/lineage/commands.sh:read
curl http://127.0.0.1:5002/api/v1/namespaces
curl http://127.0.0.1:5002/api/v1/namespaces/demo/jobs/demo-job
curl http://127.0.0.1:5002/api/v1/namespaces/demo/datasets/demo-dataset

Marquez writes the job, the run and the dataset from the events, so all three read back. The UI shows them under the demo namespace.

The UI draws the job between the datasets it read and wrote:

docs.title: From another container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, send events to http://marquez-api:5000/api/v1/lineage. For an OpenLineage client's HTTP transport, set the URL to http://marquez-api:5000, because the transport adds api/v1/lineage by default.

docs.title: MLflow tracking and model serving
docs.text:
The mlflow profile runs two containers. mlflow is the tracking server and model registry, with runs on PostgreSQL and artifacts on SeaweedFS under s3://mlflow. mlflow-serve scores a registered model over HTTP. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

odctl up mlflow
Endpoint Address Tracking UI and API from the host http://127.0.0.1:5004 Tracking API inside the odctl network http://mlflow:5000 Model server from the host http://127.0.0.1:5003/invocations Model server inside the odctl network http://mlflow-serve:5003/invocations

The server runs MLflow 3.16.1, so install the same client version on the host.

docs.title: Log a run with an artifact
docs.text:
docs/snippets/mlflow/steps.py:log-run
import pathlib
import mlflow

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://127.0.0.1:5004")
mlflow.set_experiment("demo")

p = pathlib.Path("notes.txt")
p.write_text("hello")
with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    mlflow.log_param("k", "v")
    mlflow.log_metric("m", 1.0)
    mlflow.log_artifact(str(p))

print(mlflow.get_run(run.info.run_id).info.artifact_uri)
print([f.path for f in mlflow.MlflowClient().list_artifacts(run.info.run_id)])

The artifact URI starts with mlflow-artifacts:/. The server proxies artifacts, so the client uploads through the tracking server and needs no S3 address or keys. Downloads from your machine need one setting, as Load a model from your machine shows. The run and its artifact appear in the UI.

The runs are listed under the experiment in the Model training view:

docs.title: Register a model
docs.text:
docs/snippets/mlflow/steps.py:register-model
import mlflow, numpy as np, xgboost as xgb
from mlflow import MlflowClient

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://127.0.0.1:5004")
mlflow.set_experiment("demo-model")

X, y = np.array([[0.0], [1.0], [2.0], [3.0]]), np.array([0, 0, 1, 1])
with mlflow.start_run():
    model = xgb.XGBClassifier(n_estimators=5, max_depth=2).fit(X, y)
    mlflow.xgboost.log_model(model, name="model", registered_model_name="demo-model")

client = MlflowClient()
version = max(int(mv.version) for mv in client.search_model_versions("name='demo-model'"))
client.set_registered_model_alias("demo-model", "champion", version)

This needs XGBoost on the host. The model server has XGBoost 3.2, so install the same minor version to log a model it can load.

The registry lists each version, with the champion alias on the latest:

docs.title: Serve the model
docs.text:
mlflow-serve starts with the profile and waits idle while MODEL_URI is empty. MODEL_URI is set in .odctl/.env, which odctl init writes. Change its line there to:

docs/snippets/mlflow/model-uri.env
MODEL_URI="models:/demo-model@champion"

Then run odctl up mlflow again, so the container starts with the new value, and score two rows:

docs/snippets/mlflow/commands.sh:serve
odctl up mlflow
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5003/invocations \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"inputs": [[0.0], [3.0]]}'

The response holds a predictions list, one per input row. Check the body rather than the status code, because the server answers 200 with an error payload when scoring fails. http://127.0.0.1:5003/ping answers once the model is loaded.

docs.title: Move the alias to a new version
docs.text:
mlflow-serve resolves MODEL_URI once, when its container starts. A new version registered behind an unchanged alias such as champion is not served until you run odctl restart mlflow. Nothing reports an error in the meantime, and the predictions stay those of the old version. To see the change in .env, use a version URI such as models:/demo-model/2 and run odctl up mlflow again.

Run the code from Register a model again with min_child_weight=0 added to XGBClassifier. The trees then split, so the new version predicts differently. It registers version 2 and moves champion to it. Then restart the containers and score again:

docs/snippets/mlflow/commands.sh:new-version
odctl restart mlflow
# The server answers nothing for about 16 seconds while the model loads.
until curl -fs http://127.0.0.1:5003/ping >/dev/null; do sleep 2; done
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5003/invocations \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"inputs": [[0.0], [3.0]]}'

The predictions now come from version 2: {"predictions": [0, 1]} instead of [0, 0].

docs.title: Load a model from your machine
docs.text:
Uploads go through the tracking server, but a download does not by default. The server then hands the client presigned URLs for http://seaweed:8333, a name only containers in the odctl network resolve, so mlflow.artifacts.download_artifacts and a load_model call such as mlflow.sklearn.load_model on your machine wait and print no error. Set MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD to false before the call, and the client downloads through the tracking server instead:

docs/snippets/mlflow/steps.py:download
import os

os.environ["MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD"] = "false"
import mlflow

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://127.0.0.1:5004")
path = mlflow.artifacts.download_artifacts("models:/demo-model@champion")
print(sorted(os.listdir(path)))

The output is a listing of the model files that includes MLmodel. mlflow-serve is not affected, because it loads its model inside the odctl network.

docs.title: Serve a model that reads online features
docs.text:
The MLflow image has no Feast client. A model can still read online features from feast-serve over HTTP, with an mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel whose predict method sends the request. This one reads conv_rate of the driver_stats feature view from Send rows to an HTTP API and scores a driver 1 when it is above 0.5. Start Feast with odctl up feast, apply that guide's definitions and push a value, then save the model class as driver_score.py:

docs/snippets/mlflow/driver_score.py
import mlflow
import requests


class DriverScore(mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel):
    """Scores a driver 1 when the online store holds a conversion rate above 0.5."""

    def predict(self, context, model_input, params=None):
        reply = requests.post(
            "http://feast-serve:6566/get-online-features",
            json={
                "features": ["driver_stats:conv_rate"],
                "entities": {"driver_id": [int(i) for i in model_input["driver_id"]]},
            },
            timeout=10,
        ).json()
        names = reply["metadata"]["feature_names"]
        rates = reply["results"][names.index("conv_rate")]["values"]
        return [int(rate is not None and rate > 0.5) for rate in rates]


mlflow.models.set_model(DriverScore())

Then register it from a file, so that the server loads the class from the code and not from a copy pickled on your machine. Run this in the folder that holds driver_score.py. It gives the model a signature and no input example, because an example would make MLflow call predict on your machine, where feast-serve does not resolve:

docs/snippets/mlflow/steps.py:features-model
import mlflow, pandas as pd
from mlflow import MlflowClient
from mlflow.models import infer_signature

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://127.0.0.1:5004")
mlflow.set_experiment("driver-score")
with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.pyfunc.log_model(
        name="model",
        python_model="driver_score.py",
        pip_requirements=["requests"],
        signature=infer_signature(pd.DataFrame({"driver_id": [1001]}), [1]),
        registered_model_name="driver-score",
    )

client = MlflowClient()
version = max(int(mv.version) for mv in client.search_model_versions("name='driver-score'"))
client.set_registered_model_alias("driver-score", "champion", version)

The run prints three warnings, about integer columns, type hints on predict and the missing input example, and then Created version '1' of model 'driver-score'; the warnings do not stop the registration.

Serve it as in Serve the model, with this line in .odctl/.env:

docs/snippets/mlflow/model-uri-features.env
MODEL_URI="models:/driver-score@champion"

Run odctl up mlflow again, then score the driver:

docs/snippets/mlflow/commands.sh:features-score
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5003/invocations \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"dataframe_split": {"columns": ["driver_id"], "data": [[1001]]}}'

The reply is {"predictions": [1]}. Right after apply, feast-serve may not know the feature view yet (see Send rows to an HTTP API), and the reply is an error; run the command again after a minute. The model costs one HTTP request to feast-serve for each prediction request, and mlflow-serve keeps its 1,500 MB memory limit, which a model with large libraries can reach.

docs.title: From Airflow or another container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, set the tracking URI to http://mlflow:5000 and score at http://mlflow-serve:5003/invocations. Extra Python packages for both MLflow containers go in _MLOPS_PIP_DEPS in .odctl/.env, followed by odctl recreate mlflow. Each new mlflow and mlflow-serve container downloads and installs them from PyPI again: at the first odctl up, after odctl recreate, and after odctl down and odctl up. odctl restart keeps the container, so the packages stay. Each of those starts needs PyPI, and pinned versions (transformers==5.20.2) keep the installed packages the same.

docs.title: Catalogue a database with OpenMetadata
docs.text:
The metadata profile runs OpenMetadata: the server with its UI and REST API, Elasticsearch for search, and an ingestion container, an Airflow that runs the ingestion pipelines the server deploys. Its own tables are in the omt database on PostgreSQL. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

odctl up metadata
Endpoint Address UI and REST API from the host http://127.0.0.1:8585 UI and REST API inside the odctl network http://openmetadata-server:8585 Ingestion Airflow from the host http://127.0.0.1:8087

Log in as admin@open-data.local with the password admin. The domain is open-data.local, not the upstream default, and a wrong domain fails with an invalid password error.

docs.title: Get a token
docs.text:
The login API takes the password base64-encoded and returns a JWT:

docs/snippets/openmetadata/commands.sh:login
TOKEN=$(curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"email\":\"admin@open-data.local\",\"password\":\"$(printf admin | base64)\"}" \
  http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/users/login \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["accessToken"])')
AUTH="Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

docs.title: Register PostgreSQL as a database service
docs.text:
PostgreSQL is already running, so it serves as the source. The server reaches it by its container name:

docs/snippets/openmetadata/commands.sh:service
SVC=$(curl -s -X PUT -H "$AUTH" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"demo_pg","serviceType":"Postgres","connection":{"config":{"type":"Postgres","scheme":"postgresql+psycopg2","username":"user","authType":{"password":"password"},"hostPort":"postgres:5432","database":"omt"}}}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/services/databaseServices \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["id"])')

docs.title: Run a metadata ingestion
docs.text:
Create a pipeline, deploy it as a DAG into the ingestion Airflow, and trigger it:

docs/snippets/openmetadata/commands.sh:pipeline
PIPE=$(curl -s -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"name\":\"demo_pg_metadata\",\"pipelineType\":\"metadata\",\"service\":{\"id\":\"$SVC\",\"type\":\"databaseService\"},\"sourceConfig\":{\"config\":{\"type\":\"DatabaseMetadata\"}},\"airflowConfig\":{\"startDate\":\"2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z\"}}" \
  http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/services/ingestionPipelines \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["id"])')

curl -s -X POST -H "$AUTH" http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/services/ingestionPipelines/deploy/$PIPE
curl -s -X POST -H "$AUTH" http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/services/ingestionPipelines/trigger/$PIPE

Airflow has to parse the new DAG file before the trigger works, so repeat the trigger every few seconds until it answers that the pipeline has been triggered. Then read the run's state:

docs/snippets/openmetadata/commands.sh:status
curl -s -H "$AUTH" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/services/ingestionPipelines/name/demo_pg.demo_pg_metadata?fields=pipelineStatuses"

The first entry of pipelineStatuses reaches success when the tables are catalogued. They then appear in the UI under the demo_pg service.

docs.title: Search the catalogue
docs.text:
Rebuild the search index, then query it:

docs/snippets/openmetadata/commands.sh:search
curl -s -X POST -H "$AUTH" http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/apps/trigger/SearchIndexingApplication
curl -s -H "$AUTH" "http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/search/query?q=*&index=table_search_index&size=1"

hits.total.value counts the searchable tables.

docs.title: From another container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, call the API at http://openmetadata-server:8585. The server also answers the Model Context Protocol at http://127.0.0.1:8585/mcp with the same token.

docs.title: Remove the example
docs.text:
docs/snippets/openmetadata/commands.sh:remove
curl -s -X DELETE -H "$AUTH" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/services/databaseServices/name/demo_pg?hardDelete=true&recursive=true"

docs.title: Spark
docs.text:
The spark-lite profile runs a Spark master, one worker and the Spark History Server. spark-full runs three workers. Spark's default catalog is iceberg, already pointed at the Iceberg REST catalog, so spark-sql reads and writes Iceberg tables with no extra settings. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

odctl up spark-lite
Endpoint Address Spark master UI from the host http://127.0.0.1:9080 Master URL from the host spark://127.0.0.1:7077 Spark History Server from the host http://127.0.0.1:18080 Master URL inside the odctl network spark://spark-master:7077 Spark History Server inside the odctl network http://spark-history:18080

docs.title: Run SQL against Iceberg
See finished applications
docs.text:
Every Spark application writes an event log to /tmp/spark-events, which all Spark containers share. List the logs:

docs/snippets/spark/commands.sh:event-logs
docker exec spark-master ls /tmp/spark-events

The Spark History Server at http://127.0.0.1:18080 reads the same directory, so the spark-sql run above appears there after it ends, with its jobs, stages and SQL plans. The master UI at http://127.0.0.1:9080 shows the workers and the applications the master has run.

The event logs are on a volume held in memory, so odctl down removes them.

The History Server lists the spark-sql run:

docs.title: Read a Kafka topic
docs.text:
The Kafka connector for Spark is in the shared volume with its dependencies, so a job reads Kafka with no --packages option. Start kafka-lite beside Spark, then create a topic and write three messages to it:

odctl up kafka-lite
docs/snippets/spark/commands.sh:kafka-topic
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --topic spark-demo --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1

for i in 1 2 3; do echo "{\"n\":$i}"; done | docker exec -i kafka \
  /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 --topic spark-demo

Save this PySpark job as read_kafka.py. A batch read with spark.read reads the topic from its first offset to its last and then ends:

docs/snippets/spark/read_kafka.py
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("read-kafka").getOrCreate()

df = (
    spark.read.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker-1:19092")
    .option("subscribe", "spark-demo")
    .load()
)
df.selectExpr("CAST(value AS STRING) AS value").orderBy("value").show(truncate=False)

Copy the file into the master container and submit it:

docs/snippets/spark/commands.sh:kafka-read
docker cp read_kafka.py spark-master:/tmp/read_kafka.py
docker exec spark-master /opt/spark/bin/spark-submit /tmp/read_kafka.py

The job prints a table with the values {"n":1}, {"n":2} and {"n":3}. Kafka returns each message as binary key and value columns, with the topic, partition, offset, timestamp and timestampType beside them.

docs.title: Read Avro records written with the schema registry
docs.text:
The orders topic that Flink SQL fills holds Avro records written with the Karapace schema registry. Each value is a zero byte, the 4-byte id of the schema, and then the record in Avro's binary encoding, so Spark cannot read it as text. Save this job as read_avro.py. It gets the latest schema of the subject orders-value from Karapace, drops the 5 bytes and decodes the rest with from_avro, which needs no --packages option because the Avro module is in the shared volume. This works when all records were written with the subject's latest schema version. If the Flink section has not run, the job stops with HTTP Error 404: Not Found, because the subject does not exist yet.

docs/snippets/spark/read_avro.py
import json
import urllib.request

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.avro.functions import from_avro
from pyspark.sql.functions import expr

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("read-avro").getOrCreate()

# The latest schema of the subject, as the schema registry holds it.
url = "http://karapace:8081/subjects/orders-value/versions/latest"
with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=30) as reply:
    schema = json.load(reply)["schema"]

raw = (
    spark.read.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker-1:19092")
    .option("subscribe", "orders")
    .load()
)

# Skip the first 5 bytes of each value: a zero byte and the 4-byte schema id.
orders = raw.select(
    from_avro(expr("substring(value, 6, length(value) - 5)"), schema).alias("order")
).select("order.*")
orders.orderBy("supplier", "price").show()

Copy the file into the master container and submit it:

docs/snippets/spark/commands.sh:avro-read
docker cp read_avro.py spark-master:/tmp/read_avro.py
docker exec spark-master /opt/spark/bin/spark-submit /tmp/read_avro.py

The job prints a table with the columns supplier and price, and the rows a 5.0, a 10.0 and b 7.5.

docs.title: From another container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, submit applications to spark://spark-master:7077. Spark's settings, including the iceberg catalog and S3 access to SeaweedFS, are in spark/spark-defaults.conf in the workspace.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
The telemetry profile runs the grafana/otel-lgtm image: an OpenTelemetry Collector, Prometheus, Tempo, Loki and Grafana in one container. Start it next to the profiles you want to watch:

odctl up telemetry kafka-lite flink-lite

Endpoint Address Grafana (user user, password password) http://127.0.0.1:3004 Prometheus http://127.0.0.1:19090 OTLP through the collector 127.0.0.1:4317 (gRPC), http://127.0.0.1:4318 (HTTP)

docs.title: Where the metrics come from
docs.text: Prometheus scrapes the services that publish a metrics endpoint, by container name on the odctl network. Airflow pushes its metrics over OTLP to the collector, and the collector reads PostgreSQL and Valkey directly. A service that is not running is simply a target that is down.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text:
Grafana has a dashboard per service in a folder named odctl. A dashboard fills in once its service's profile is up. The dashboards are JSON files in .odctl/grafana/dashboards/. Edit a file and run odctl restart telemetry to load it. Changes made in the Grafana UI are not kept.

For example, the PostgreSQL dashboard:

docs.title: Send your own metrics
docs.text:
Point an OpenTelemetry SDK at http://127.0.0.1:4318, its default HTTP port. The end-to-end tests post one metric with curl, which shows the path:

docs/snippets/telemetry/commands.sh:send-metric
ts=$(python3 -c "import time;print(int(time.time()*1e9))")
cat > /tmp/otlp.json <<JSON
{"resourceMetrics":[{"resource":{"attributes":[{"key":"service.name","value":{"stringValue":"demo"}}]},
"scopeMetrics":[{"scope":{"name":"demo"},"metrics":[{"name":"demo_total","unit":"1",
"sum":{"aggregationTemporality":2,"isMonotonic":true,"dataPoints":[
{"asDouble":42,"timeUnixNano":"${ts}","startTimeUnixNano":"${ts}","attributes":[]}]}}]}]}]}
JSON
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data-binary @/tmp/otlp.json \
  http://127.0.0.1:4318/v1/metrics
curl "http://127.0.0.1:19090/api/v1/query?query=demo_total"

Prometheus also accepts OTLP metrics directly at http://127.0.0.1:19090/api/v1/otlp/v1/metrics.

docs.title: Temporal workers
docs.text:
The temporal profile runs the Temporal development server: the server, the Web UI and a SQLite database in one container. odctl runs only the server. Your own process runs the worker that executes workflows and activities. The end-to-end tests run the code below on every release.

docs/snippets/temporal-workers/commands.sh:install
odctl up temporal
pip install temporalio==1.34.0

The gRPC endpoint is 127.0.0.1:7233 with the namespace default, and the Web UI is at http://127.0.0.1:8233.

docs.title: A worker and a workflow
docs.text:
The activity fails on its first attempt, so the result shows that the retry policy ran it again.

docs/snippets/temporal-workers/steps.py:worker
import asyncio
from datetime import timedelta
from temporalio import activity, workflow
from temporalio.client import Client
from temporalio.common import RetryPolicy
from temporalio.worker import Worker


@activity.defn
async def greet(name: str) -> str:
    if activity.info().attempt < 2:
        raise RuntimeError("first attempt fails on purpose")
    return f"hello {name}"


@workflow.defn
class Greet:
    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, name: str) -> str:
        return await workflow.execute_activity(
            greet, name,
            start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(seconds=30),
            retry_policy=RetryPolicy(initial_interval=timedelta(seconds=1), maximum_attempts=3),
        )


async def main() -> None:
    client = await Client.connect("127.0.0.1:7233")
    async with Worker(client, task_queue="demo", workflows=[Greet], activities=[greet]):
        print(await client.execute_workflow(Greet.run, "odctl", id="greet-1", task_queue="demo"))


# The workflow sandbox imports this file again, so run main only as a script.
if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Wait for an approval
docs.text:
A workflow can wait for a signal, for example a person approving an agent's action. The workflow below waits until its approve signal arrives, and then returns who approved it:

docs/snippets/temporal-workers/steps.py:approval-workflow
@workflow.defn
class Approval:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.approver = None

    @workflow.signal
    def approve(self, approver: str) -> None:
        self.approver = approver

    @workflow.run
    async def run(self) -> str:
        await workflow.wait_condition(lambda: self.approver is not None)
        return f"approved by {self.approver}"

In main above, register it with the worker, start it, then send the signal:

docs/snippets/temporal-workers/steps.py:approval-run
async with Worker(client, task_queue="demo", workflows=[Greet, Approval], activities=[greet]):
    handle = await client.start_workflow(Approval.run, id="approval-1", task_queue="demo")
    await handle.signal(Approval.approve, "alice")
    print(await handle.result())

Until the signal arrives, the Web UI lists the workflow as running.

The Web UI at http://127.0.0.1:8233 lists each workflow. Here approval-2 was started without a signal, so it is still running:

docs.title: History
docs.text: Workflow history is in the database file inside the container. It survives odctl restart temporal, and the tests check that a workflow left waiting for its signal resumes and completes afterwards. odctl down removes the history, as it removes every odctl service's data.

docs.title: Trino and Metabase
docs.text:
The trino profile runs Trino, which queries PostgreSQL, Iceberg, ClickHouse, Kafka and Valkey through one SQL interface. The metabase profile runs Metabase, which draws charts and dashboards over those databases. Metabase keeps its own settings and dashboards in PostgreSQL, so both profiles start postgres. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

odctl up trino metabase
Endpoint Address Trino UI and JDBC from the host http://127.0.0.1:8080 Metabase from the host http://127.0.0.1:3000

docs.title: Trino catalogs
docs.text:
docs/snippets/trino-metabase/commands.sh:catalogs
docker exec trino trino --execute "SHOW CATALOGS"
Catalog Reads Needs postgres the odctl database nothing more iceberg tables in the REST catalog, with files on SeaweedFS catalog clickhouse the feature_store database on ch-11 ch-lite or ch-full kafka topics, with fields from the Karapace schema registry kafka-lite or kafka-full valkey keys in Valkey valkey

Every catalog loads when Trino starts, even when its service is not running. A query against such a catalog fails until you start that profile. Catalogs finish loading after Trino's health endpoint starts answering, so SHOW CATALOGS can take a minute to list them all.

Run a query:

docs/snippets/trino-metabase/commands.sh:query
docker exec trino trino --execute "SELECT 1"

Trino has no password authentication, so it accepts any user name. docker exec -it trino trino connects as trino. Pass --user user to use the name the rest of the stack uses. Workspace explains the access rules in trino/rules.json.

The Trino UI at http://127.0.0.1:8080 asks only for a user name. It shows the cluster and the queries that ran in the last few minutes.

docs.title: Metabase
docs.text:
Open http://127.0.0.1:3000 and create the first admin account. Then add each database under Admin settings, Databases, with these settings:

Database type Host Port Other settings PostgreSQL postgres 5432 database odctl, user user, password password ClickHouse ch-11 8123 database default, user default, password password, no SSL Starburst (for Trino) trino 8080 catalog postgres, schema public, user admin, no SSL

Metabase runs inside the odctl network, so it reaches each database by container name. Use the Starburst driver for Trino, because it is the Trino driver Metabase ships. It needs a catalog, and any catalog in the table above works.

Metabase takes a while to start. It is ready when this request succeeds:

docs/snippets/trino-metabase/commands.sh:metabase-health
curl http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/health

A SQL question on the PostgreSQL connection, shown as a bar chart:

docs.text: Inside the odctl network, Trino is at http://trino:8080 and Metabase at http://metabase:3000.

docs.title: Valkey
docs.text:
The valkey profile runs the Valkey Bundle image as one container named valkey. The registry describes it as a cache and data store with JSON, Bloom and vector search capabilities. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

odctl up valkey
Setting Value Address from the host 127.0.0.1:6379 Address inside the odctl network valkey:6379 User user, password password Memory limit 512 MB

docs.title: Users and permissions
docs.text: The unauthenticated default user is turned off, so every client logs in as user. That user has every command, every key pattern and every Pub/Sub channel. Channels are a separate permission in Valkey, and the profile grants them explicitly, so PUBLISH and SUBSCRIBE work as well as key commands.

docs.title: Write and read keys
docs.text:
valkey-cli is in the container. Log in with a URL that carries the user and password:

docs/snippets/valkey/commands.sh:round-trip
vk=redis://user:password@localhost:6379
docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" ping
docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" mset 'model:1' '{"a":1}' 'model:2' '{"a":2}'
docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" mget 'model:1' 'model:2'
docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" del 'model:1' 'model:2'

--no-auth-warning stops valkey-cli printing a warning about the password on the command line. ping answers PONG. mset writes both keys in one command, and mget reads them back in one round trip, which is how product-recommender stores and loads its models.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text: Valkey writes an append-only file and saves a snapshot every 60 seconds when at least one key has changed. Both files are inside the container, so a restart keeps the data and odctl down removes it.

docs.title: From another container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, connect to valkey:6379 with the same user and password, for example redis://user:password@valkey:6379 for a Redis client. Feast's online store uses this address, as Feast with Iceberg shows.

docs.title: trino
docs.text:

  configured, so any username is accepted):
  * External (host): http://127.0.0.1:8080
  * Internal (Docker): http://trino:8080
• Identities: `docker exec -it trino trino` connects as `trino`, the
  CLI default. Pass `--user user` for the stack-wide convention, or
  `--user analyst`, which trino/rules.json denies schema ownership
  while leaving every table privilege in place.

  kafka, clickhouse and valkey load without their backing services,

  catalog, storage, kafka-lite, ch-lite or valkey is also up.
